finding.claim: PUT /doc/<doc_id> (update_doc) never enforces edit permission: can_edit() is called as a bare statement and its boolean result is discarded, so any caller who reaches the handler can overwrite the body of any document, including documents they neither own nor are listed as editors on.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled doc_id in the URL path (docs.py:17) and request.json['body'] (docs.py:20). Precondition: the request has an authenticated g.user (set outside this file; not verified here). No owner/editor constraint is applied to the lookup.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] (docs.py:20), a write to a protected document owned by another user.

trace.note: Route registered for PUT /doc/<doc_id>; no decorator or auth check in this file.
doc_id taken from attacker-controlled URL path.
doc = DOCS[doc_id]; object fetched by id with no owner/editor scoping.
can_edit(g.user, doc) evaluated as a bare statement; result is neither tested nor used, so no abort(403) occurs.
can_edit returns a bool (owner == user or user in editors) and has no side effects, so the discarded result cannot gate anything.
Unconditionally writes attacker-supplied body into the document.
Contrast: update_title correctly uses require_edit(), which aborts with 403 — confirming the intended control was omitted in update_doc.

finding.guards_checked: (1) Return value of can_edit at docs.py:19 — not used as a gate; (2) require_edit / abort(403) — absent from update_doc; (3) route-level auth decorators or before_request hooks — none in docs.py (g.user population not visible, so authentication status is an unverified precondition); (4) owner/tenant scoping on DOCS lookup at docs.py:18 — none, so the object is found by id alone. Matches expertise case 01-perm-result-ignored. Decoy check: not a decoy — the predicate is a pure function whose result is simply ignored, which is the vulnerable pattern. Not a finding: update_title (docs.py:24-29) correctly enforces require_edit before writing.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only permission predicate used in update_doc is can_edit (docs.py:7-8), called as a bare statement at docs.py:19 with its bool discarded, so no abort occurs. The working directory contains only docs.py, so no before_request or auth decorator exists in scope; require_edit (docs.py:11-13) is used only by update_title (docs.py:27).
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches: update_doc at docs.py:16-21 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) at line 19 without testing the result, so the body write at line 20 runs for any caller who reaches the handler, while update_title at line 27 correctly uses require_edit. The attacker only needs whatever access the app grants any request (an authenticated user per the claim, or even anonymous if g.user is None, since the check does not block either way), and the write is not blocked by any control in this codebase.
